sarcastic

/sar-KASS-tik/ - the stress falls on KASS · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sarcastic means mocking by saying the opposite of what is meant.

'Love what the fog did to the view,' read the resort guestbook's most sarcastic entry.

Worked Example

The scout troop's map skills failed at the second fork, and by nightfall the 'shortcut' had added six miles. As they finally limped into camp, Ruiz surveyed his blistered crew and announced, 'Outstanding navigation, gentlemen. Truly, the compass was only slowing us down.' Nobody thought he meant a word of it — which was precisely the point.

Sarcastic is the exact word because the mockery runs through reversal: he says 'outstanding' and means 'disastrous,' and the gap between the two is where the sting lives. Plain criticism would say 'we got lost'; fond teasing would keep the warmth in it. Sarcasm hands you praise with the poles reversed and trusts you to feel the shock.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

snide: Snide remarks are sneering put-downs that don't bother with the reversal — the contempt is said straight out. Sarcastic mockery wears praise-shaped words and means their opposite, trusting the tone to flip them. If the insult never dresses up as a compliment, it is snide rather than sarcastic.

wry: Wry is dry, tilted humor — amusement without the wound, often pointed at oneself or at life's small absurdities. Sarcastic wit says the opposite of what it means and wants the sting to land. A wry remark keeps the crooked smile; a sarcastic one sharpens it into a jab.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

sincere: means exactly what it says

straightforward: says the thing plainly, with no double floor

Where it sits · how hostile the wit has turned — teasing → sarcastic → withering

teasing vs. sarcastic: Teasing pokes fun and stays fond — the target is in on the joke; sarcastic sharpens it, and the target is the joke.

withering vs. sarcastic: Withering goes past sarcastic: the sarcastic reply still wears a joke's clothing, while the withering one drops the costume and simply scorches.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — sarc

Root — sarc: flesh

Suffix — -astic

Suffix — -astic: given to, marked by

Put it together

Put it together: Sarc (flesh, from Greek sarx) + -astic (given to, as in enthusiastic) = given to flesh-tearing. Greek sarkazein meant 'to rend flesh the way dogs do,' and Greek speakers borrowed it for speech that bites. Every sarcastic remark keeps the family resemblance: humor with teeth in it.

Word Choice

everyday / edged

Sarcastic is mockery by reversal — praise-shaped words with the meaning inverted, tone doing the signaling. It ranges from locker-room fond to genuinely cruel, so read the room twice. Kin worth keeping straight: wry is the gentle, self-aware tilt; snide sneers without the wit; and a deadpan delivery is a technique — sarcasm's favorite mask — not an attitude.
